message.content:
The sea typically looks **blue**—a result of how water absorbs and scatters sunlight. Water molecules absorb longer wavelengths (red, orange, yellow) more strongly than shorter wavelengths (blue, violet). The remaining blue light is scattered in all directions, giving the ocean its characteristic hue.

However, the exact color can change depending on several factors:

| Factor | Effect on Color |
|--------|-----------------|
| **Depth** | Deeper water tends to appear darker blue or even greenish‑blue because more light is absorbed. |
| **Algae & phytoplankton** | High concentrations can give the water a green or turquoise tint. |
| **Sediment & turbidity** | Suspended particles can make the water look brownish or murky. |
| **Sun angle & weather** | Low sun angles (sunrise/sunset) can produce warm hues (orange, pink), while overcast skies may make the sea appear grayish. |
| **Ice & snow** | In polar regions, the sea can appear pale blue or even white when covered with ice. |

So while “blue” is the most common descriptor, the sea’s color is actually a dynamic spectrum influenced by environmental conditions.
